articles.title: CoAP: 2,188,380 answers for a protocol designed to be spoken to by anything
articles.excerpt: CoAP: 2,188,380 answers for a protocol designed to be spoken to by anything A ZoomEye query for service="coap" returned 2,188,380 matches on 28 October 2026. CoAP is the Constrained Application Protoc…
articles.body: CoAP: 2,188,380 answers for a protocol designed to be spoken to by anything A ZoomEye query for service="coap" returned 2,188,380 matches on 28 October 2026. CoAP is the Constrained Application Protocol, standardised as RFC 7252 in 2014, and it was built for devices that cannot afford TLS handshakes or verbose headers: sensors, meters, building controllers, industrial gateways. Every one of those 2.19 million answers is a UDP endpoint that will parse a request from whoever sends one. What the query selects service="coap" asks ZoomEye to report hosts where the probe recognised CoAP semantics rather than a bare port number. That distinction matters, because CoAP runs on UDP 5683 with no connection handshake and no banner.

articles.title: How 'spacewalking' underwater made me feel like I was really in space
articles.excerpt: Analog Astronaut Commander and Aquanaut Michaela Musilova led underwater simulated “spacewalks” in low visibility to test astronaut safety and communication protocols during simulated space missions.
articles.body: I was breathing just fine through my life support systems, but I kept feeling an urge to double check that everything was ok with my "spacesuit" before heading out on this "spacewalk." I have worn many different types of spacesuits on Earth during my career, but for the first time in my life, I knew that I couldn’t just stop to breathe the air outside if there were an emergency. That's because I was underwater. On this excursion, I was leading a simulated space mission underwater called SEA STAR. My " spacesuit " was actually scuba diving gear, and the simulated spacewalks , or EVAs (Extra-Vehicular Activities), included outings where we explored underwater environments.

articles.body: A passage can be relevant to a question and still be unsuitable for the response the system is preparing. An internal exception procedure might explain how a team works without granting permission to promise that exception to a customer. An old instruction might be semantically close to the query while no longer carrying authority. This is why the operational retrieval blueprint in my portfolio includes allowed-use metadata. The public artifact is a starter design with schema, synthetic documents, and evaluation questions. It is not proof of a fully deployed knowledge service or a measured improvement in answers. Relevance answers only part of the question A retriever ranks text according to a query and its scoring method.

articles.title: LicenseTrace: Exhuming the Forgotten Evidence Behind Software Licenses
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine Modern AI coding agents frequently inspect open-source repositories to install packages, import helpers…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built Modern AI coding agents frequently inspect open-source repositories to install packages, import helpers, or borrow design patterns. When an agent does this, it relies on a fragile heuristic: it checks if a root LICENSE file exists or reads the "license" field in package.json . If it finds MIT , the agent assumes the code is safe to use. Open-source repositories are rarely that clean. They carry historical ghosts: Deleted licenses: A repository began life under GPL-3.0 in 2018, but a maintainer deleted the license file in 2021 without obtaining relicensing consent from previous contributors. The original terms still exist in the Git commit database.

articles.title: Still Charging: The Zombie Subscriptions That Keep Coming Back
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine A subscription can outlive the reason it started. A free trial ends. A price changes. A service you mea…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine A subscription can outlive the reason it started. A free trial ends. A price changes. A service you meant to cancel keeps appearing on the statement. Still Charging helps you spot those recurring charges and decide what to do with them—without connecting to your bank or handing your statement to an AI service. What I Built Still Charging is a privacy-first subscription review tool. Import a CSV or text-based PDF bank statement, and the app looks for recurring charges and possible price increases. It shows the evidence behind each candidate: the observed dates and amounts, the estimated billing cadence, and a confidence label. The pattern is still only a suspicion until you review it.

articles.title: Entity Consistency for AI Search: Same Name, Same City, Same Service List
articles.excerpt: Generative engines build answers by stitching passages from your site and from third parties. When those sources disagree about who you are, the model often hedges — or picks a competitor with cleaner…
articles.body: Generative engines build answers by stitching passages from your site and from third parties. When those sources disagree about who you are, the model often hedges — or picks a competitor with cleaner facts. Entity consistency is the boring prerequisite behind many GEO wins. The fields that must match Across your homepage, About page, footer, directories and major profiles, align: Legal or trading name (and one clear brand name) Headquarters city / region Founding year (if you publish it) Core services in the same order of emphasis Markets served (e.g. overseas merchants only) Contact email and phone formats Logo variants that still look like one brand You do not need identical marketing copy everywhere. You need identical facts .

articles.title: Astronomers discover the secrets of 'string of pearls' supernova relic and the zombie star at its heart
articles.excerpt: Scientists are still learning about a cosmic 'string of pearls,' a unique celestial relic left by a supernova witnessed by humanity around 850 years ago, which has a zombie star at its heart.
articles.body: Scientists are still learning about a cosmic "string of pearls," a unique celestial relic left by a supernova explosion that humanity witnessed around 850 years ago. That is thanks to the most detailed observation of the dandelion-shaped chains of gas and supernova debris that comprise Pa 30, the only supernova remnant of its type observed in the Milky Way . What makes Pa 30 even more unique is that it has a rare "zombie star" at its heart. Supernovas like the one that created Pa 30 are called Type Ia supernovas; they happen when a dead star called a white dwarf overfeeds on a companion star like a cosmic vampire. This overfeeding triggers a runaway nuclear explosion that usually destroys the white dwarf.

articles.title: Cowboy Space unveils 'Big Iron' rocket to launch 20,000 AI data centers
articles.excerpt: Cowboy Space just gave us our first look at its "Big Iron" rocket, which the company will use to build its AI data center constellation. Big Iron's debut is targeted for late 2028.
articles.body: PALO ALTO, Calif. — Cowboy Space just showed us how it plans to become a big player in the final frontier. The California-based company, which is run by Robinhood co-founder Baiju Bhatt, intends to operate a constellation of 20,000 AI data centers in low Earth orbit (LEO). It will build those satellites in house and launch them on a homegrown rocket — a vehicle Cowboy Space unveiled here on Monday night (Oct. 26), at an event it called "Big Sky Rising." "It's a fundamentally novel approach to rocketry in the modern era, in our opinion," Bhatt said during the event. "The idea is that you have a two-stage rocket where the upper stage of the rocket itself transforms into the satellite." Big Iron's first stage will be reusable.

articles.title: November full moon 2026: When, where and how to see the Beaver Moon
articles.excerpt: Your guide to November's full Beaver Moon, from peak times to skywatching highlights.
articles.body: The November full moon reaches maximum illumination at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk sits opposite the sun in Earth's sky, appearing fully lit by its rays. November's full moon is traditionally known as the " Beaver Moon ", because it rises around the time when the small mammals take refuge in their dens, having stored enough food to survive the long winter months, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . The Nov. 24 full moon also happens to be the first of three consecutive " supermoons ". The non-scientific term is often bestowed on full moons that occur when the natural satellite is within 90% of perigee, when the moon is closest to Earth in its elliptical orbit.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 27, 1961: NASA launches Saturn I rocket on 1st test flight from Florida to set stage for the mighty Saturn V moon rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 27, 1961, NASA launched the first test flight of its new Saturn I space launch vehicle. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 27, 1961, NASA launched the first test flight of its new Saturn I space launch vehicle. The Saturn I rocket was the United States' first heavy-lift rocket designed to launch big payloads beyond low Earth orbit. This was also the first test flight of any rocket in the Saturn family of rockets, which includes the Saturn V that was used to launch astronauts to the moon during the Apollo program . The Saturn I was enormous compared to every rocket that came before it. It was almost three times as tall as the Jupiter-C rocket, which launched the first American satellite into orbit in 1958. It also produced more than 10 times the amount of thrust that the Jupiter-C rocket could. The liquid-powered rocket launched on its maiden voyage from Cape Canaveral.
